issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette:
Leilani had always thought of her body as a reliable tool, as sturdy and dependable as the welding torch she had wielded for over fifty years. At eighty, she still took pride in the strength of her hands and the steadiness of her gaze. That all changed six months ago. An argument with her husband, Fa'a, over something trivial—money for a grandchild’s birthday—had escalated with a terrifying speed. In the midst of the shouting, he had shoved her. It wasn’t a gentle push; it was a violent, two-handed thrust that sent her stumbling backward. She lost her footing and fell hard, the sharp corner of their koa wood dining table catching her hip with a sickening crack. The physical pain was immediate and searing, but it was the shock of Fa’a’s face, contorted with a rage she had never seen in five decades of marriage, that fractured something deeper.

Her recovery from the broken hip was slow and arduous, a period during which a set of unshakeable beliefs took root. Leilani became convinced that the injury was not temporary; to her, it was a permanent failing. She had come to believe her body was irrevocably damaged, a belief that haunted her long after the cast came off. Every lingering ache, every moment of stiffness, was proof that she could no longer trust her own body to support her. This profound sense of physical vulnerability bled into every aspect of her life, transforming her home from a sanctuary into a source of constant threat. Because she saw her body as fragile and broken, every creak of the floorboards at night sounded like a footstep, and the familiar silhouette of her husband sleeping beside her offered no comfort. She felt perpetually on guard, even locked inside her own home, certain that her weakened frame could not withstand another accident or assault.

The nights became a landscape of fear. Sleep was a shallow, unreliable state she could rarely maintain for more than an hour at a time. She would often wake with a jolt, heart pounding, straining her ears in the darkness to check whether she was safe. This constant state of high alert, the relentless vigilance and broken sleep, began to erode her from the inside. The sheer exhaustion left her feeling frail and unsteady on her feet during the day, which only served as confirmation of her deepest fear: that her body had failed her for good. The unending anxiety also scoured away her ability to feel anything else. Joy, contentment, even sadness felt like distant memories. This emotional numbness was terrifying; it was as if the fall had shaken loose her capacity for normal feelings, leaving her to conclude that she would never be able to feel them again.

This vicious cycle now governs her existence. Her belief in her own permanent damage fuels a state of constant threat, and that state of threat, in turn, provides daily evidence for her bleak appraisals. She tried to return to her welding workshop in the garage, hoping the familiar heat and hiss of the torch would ground her. But she found she couldn’t hold the equipment steady, and the sudden flare of the arc made her flinch violently. The work that had defined her strength now only amplified her sense of weakness and unreliability. She has since refused all commissions, retreating further into the quiet of her house, a place she no longer feels is her own.

It was her daughter who finally convinced her to seek help, alarmed at seeing her once-vibrant mother become a ghost in her own home. Leilani came to her first session without hope, her posture stooped with a weariness that was more than physical. She explained that Fa’a was consumed by shame and remorse, but his presence was a constant, living reminder of her body’s betrayal. What she wanted to know, she said quietly, was whether it was possible to ever feel safe in your own skin again after it has been broken, or if this feeling of being a fragile, guarded stranger in her own life was now her permanent reality.
